newsitem.title: TURKEY: Turkish cabinet meets over army Islamist warning.
newsitem.headline: Turkish cabinet meets over army Islamist warning.

text.p: Turkey's Islamist-led cabinet meets on Thursday to consider army demands to curb religious activism and return the country to rigid secularism.

"It is natural for the MGK (National Security Council) to give us advice. The government will first discuss this advice and follow through sections that are compatible with the government programme," said Oguzhan Asilturk, a senior member of Prime Minister Necmettin Erbakan's Welfare Party.
"And the reasons for not following through the parts that are not compatible will be announced to the public," Asilturk was quoted as saying by the state-run Anatolian news agency.

Erbakan, the first Islamist to lead modern Turkey, has signed a declaration by the powerful MGK -- which comprises senior military and government figures plus the president -- recommending a crackdown against recent Islamist zeal that the generals fear undermines official secularism and democracy.

Tourism Minister Bahattin Yucel, of the pro-Western junior coalition partner, the True Path Party, told Reuters the cabinet would discuss the MGK's proposed measures in the meeting and go some way to putting them into practice.
The military objected to measures planned by Erbakan's government to relax laws on Islamic headgear in public sector workplaces and to build mosques in secular strongholds.
The regularly scheduled MGK meeting a week and a half ago came amid speculation in Turkey's strongly secularist press that the army could be preparing for its fourth coup since 1960.

Erbakan has failed to muster support against the declaration from among the pro-secular parties -- even True Path. He has since slammed them for being "secular fascists", "ignorant" enough to pose secularism against religion, and presented himself as the true guardian of democracy.

But the prime minister has nevertheless said the cabinet meeting would "show all due care and attention" to a military order for a revival of the rigid secularism of the 1920s, when the republic rose from the ashes of the Ottoman Empire.
Political analysts say Erbakan will probably give concessions at Thursday's meeting on demands that he does not see as directly affecting his grassroots support.

Commentators say that without upsetting his Islamist voters he can bring illegal Koranic instruction under official control and license tens of thousands of shotguns that the army fears may be used by religious militants.
The generals want the coalition to legislate against peaceful Islamist dissent and restrict the number of religious secondary schools where many Welfare supporters were educated.

The army's latest involvement in politics has strained the unity of the coalition, formed last June after months of bargaining. Welfare won a narrow victory with 21 percent of the vote at general elections in 1995.
